dom.t: Model providers: Suppliers now compete for workflows

st.t: Model providers: Suppliers now compete for workflows
st.an: Barnes accepts that Claude is becoming a configurable legal-workflow layer and adds concrete early demonstrations of practice-specific plugins, connectors and firm-level customization. He also reinforces the cluster’s limitation that this shifts production work rather than replacing lawyer judgment, though his effectiveness claims rest on brief hands-on use rather than systematic evaluation.

st.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment
st.an: Barnes accepts the need for use-case-specific deployment and extends it with concrete connector-level implementation controls: verify that an integration supports the intended task, then assess non-native connectors handling firm data for security, traceability and software-supply-chain risks. This materially develops the cluster’s workflow-redesign and continuous, context-specific governance propositions.
qs: So, you're going to make sure that what you need to do is available and possible to do.
And if you do decide that you want to use an MCP or a non-native connector, there's six things that I want you to look at and think about.

st.t: General platforms: Legal procedure may defend specialists
st.an: Barnes supports the cluster’s view that Claude is becoming foundational infrastructure for practice-specific legal workflows while stopping short of autonomous practice. He presents rapid setup and production capabilities as useful, but expressly retains attorney judgment and review for every output; his platform-level conclusions are partly inferential rather than proof of specialist displacement.
qs: Every output is a draft for attorney review.
Thomson Reuters, the company that obviously owns Casetext, one of the biggest legal AI products in the world, rebuilt Casetext on top of the Claude agent SDK.

kp.k: Practice-specific plugins replace a general-purpose legal workflow package
kp.d: Barnes describes a release made the day before recording, which he informally calls Claude for Legal 2.0, as a rebuild comprising 12 plugins and 22 integrations or connectors. He contrasts the earlier general-purpose plugin with practice-specific skills, setup interviews, preference files and software connections. These are his launch observations after approximately 24–36 hours of use, not a systematic evaluation; he expressly acknowledges that some practice areas remain uncovered.
qs: Not a version bump, it was really a rebuild.
There's still plenty of practice areas that are not included, but litigation has 19 skills from memory. Uh employment has 20. IP has 12.
Every plugin ships with its own setup interview, its own preference file, and its own connection points into the software that you're already paying for.

kp.k: Customization encodes firm procedures before workflows execute
kp.d: Barnes identifies a 10–15-minute initial interview covering jurisdiction, matter types, output formats and reviewers as the mechanism for tailoring outputs. Answers become a preference file read by every skill, embedding firm voice, checklists and rules. He argues that this improves output quality and remedies a weakness of the first plugin; workflows can then be invoked through natural language or slash commands.
qs: Cloe asks you about your practice, what jurisdiction, what types of matters, what output formats your firm uses, who reviews everything at the end.
Takes 10 to 15 minutes to go through it.
Every skill in the plugin reads that file before it does anything else. Your firm's voice, your firm's checklist, your firm's rules.

kp.k: Workflow coverage spans firms, in-house teams and legal education
kp.d: Barnes describes commercial, corporate and employment workflows for in-house counsel, including contract review, M&A due diligence, board minutes, entity compliance, hiring and investigations. For firms, he highlights litigation intake, chronologies, drafting, privilege review and deposition preparation, alongside IP clearance and infringement-related work. Student and clinic plugins cover bar preparation, IRAC, intake, deadlines and supervisor review queues. These are described capabilities rather than measured educational or service outcomes.
qs: So, commercial for contract reviews, NDAs, MSAs, escalations, corporate, you've got M&A due diligence, board minutes, entity compliance, uh employment for hiring, terminations, investigations, leave tracking, and so on and so forth.
Matter intake, chronology building, demand drafting, privilege log review, deposition preparation, brief section drafting.
The law student skill handles bar prep, IRAC, among other things. Legal clinic handles client intake, deadlines, supervisor review queues, and so on and so forth.

kp.k: Lawyers retain judgment and review responsibility
kp.d: Barnes frames the technology as substituting for operations and production work while augmenting, rather than replacing, lawyers' judgment. He says attorney review is required for every output, attributing that position both to Anthropic and the plugins. His proposed drafting workflow includes marking up the result and sending it to a partner, much as with an associate's first draft.
qs: Every output is a draft for attorney review.
Anthropic says it, the plugin says it, I'm saying it.
AI doesn't replace your great judgment, and that stays with you.
You'd read it, I guess mark it up, send it to a partner, same as you would with an associate's first attempt.

kp.k: Reported partnerships position Claude as legal infrastructure
kp.d: Barnes reports 20,000 registrations for an April Anthropic legal webinar, a Freshfields co-innovation agreement, Quinn Emanuel's internally built litigation platform and Thomson Reuters rebuilding Casetext on Claude's agent SDK. He attributes the absence of a coding background to the Quinn Emanuel partner who led that project and a greater focus on expert judgment to Crosby Legal. His suggestion that these relationships shaped the release is explicitly speculative.

That's a blue-chip firm betting on Claude as a foundation partner, not just a tool.
Quinn Emanuel built their own internal litigation platform on top of Claude. And the partner who led it actually said that they didn't have any coding background.

And this is just me reading between the lines, but I think this release today is probably what Claude has been learning through these conversations and these partnerships with these types of firms.

kp.k: Missing native integrations create implementation costs and constraints
kp.d: Barnes says Clio, Centerbase, PracticePanther, MyCase and Smokeball lack native launch connectors. Firms must instead use bridges such as Zapier or available or custom MCP connections, whose read/write capabilities vary. He describes additional accounts, costs, individual authentication and deployment work, recommending Zapier as easier for legal teams while noting that functionality requirements may necessitate another MCP.

And so, that's a setup process, that's an additional cost.
And of the two, Zapier is much easier for for a legal team.

kp.k: Connector governance requires security, permissions and liability checks
kp.d: Barnes recommends six checks for non-native connections to firm data: data residency, credential storage, audit trails, supply-chain and code review, scope minimization, and liability allocation. He also recommends cybersecurity scanning, sandbox testing and matching deployment choices to internal capability and risk tolerance. His suggestion that an ABA AI opinion, tentatively recalled as 512, makes audit logging nearly mandatory is expressly a non-lawyer's interpretation, not a quoted professional rule.
qs: Some MCPs round trip data through a third-party server. Some run locally on your machine.
Can you point to a log that shows an audit log of every call that was made by who, when, with what payload, essentially what information was passed through.
The ABA's new opinion, from memory, I think 512, I'm not a lawyer, um, on AI makes use case of this close to mandatory, I would say.
Only grant permissions the workflow actually needs.
Now, building your own gives you full control, but you also own everything that breaks.

kp.k: Intake demonstration links document analysis to matter-system updates
kp.d: Using a mock complaint and client narrative, Barnes demonstrates extracting parties, claims, jurisdiction and facts, then requesting creation of a Clio matter. The system asks permission before creation and populates matter information and notes without manual re-entry. Although he initially presents Zapier as the easier demonstration route, he observes that the completed action used the Clio MCP, advising users with both connections to specify the desired connector.

And you'll see here it's asking for permission to allow the matter creation.
So, you can see there the matter type is set, all the parties are filled in, it's got detailed notes.
I didn't come over to Clio and type it in.
you'll see here it says that it used the Clio MCP.

kp.k: Junior-time savings are illustrated through hypothetical billing arithmetic
kp.d: Barnes estimates that a chronology would take a junior associate about 2 hours and multiplies this by 200 active matters annually and a $400 hourly blended rate to suggest $160,000 of junior time largely automated per attorney per year. This is an illustrative extrapolation accompanying a demonstration, not a measured saving across firms. He also describes chaining intake and chronology into demand-letter drafting that flags partner-review sections and jurisdictional assumptions.

kp.k: Live research connector supports a first-pass trademark memo
kp.d: Barnes demonstrates an IP clearance workflow for a startup's proposed Northwind mark using the native Free Law Project/CourtListener connector. He describes live searches for disputes involving similar marks, federal case law and citation networks, contrasting API retrieval with reliance on model training data. He reports a detailed first-pass memo in three or four minutes, possibly longer, against his tentative estimate that such a question can occupy half an associate's day. The demonstration does not report a systematic assessment of accuracy or completeness.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: Barnes claims practice-specific Claude plugins make customised legal production workflows accessible with limited technical expertise, while leaving legal judgment and review with lawyers.
pts.d: Barnes characterises the release as a rebuild rather than an incremental update: 12 practice-area plugins and 22 connectors replace a more general-purpose starting point with practice-specific skills, setup interviews and persistent firm preferences. He claims these tools can take over substantial operations and production work, not the lawyer's judgment. Despite the opening 'kill switch' rhetoric, his concrete account is of supervised automation rather than autonomous replacement of lawyers.

pts.k: Barnes claims connected workflows automate matter administration and substantially reduce junior drafting and chronology work.
pts.d: In his litigation demonstration, Barnes describes extracting parties, claims, jurisdiction and facts from a mock complaint and client narrative, then creating and populating a Clio matter following permission. He also describes chronology generation and a subsequent demand-letter workflow. His illustrative calculation values largely automated chronology work at $160,000 of junior time annually per attorney, assuming two hours per chronology, 200 active matters and a $400 hourly rate. This is a hypothetical valuation of time, not a reported measurement of cash savings, revenue effects or job losses.

pts.k: Barnes claims live research connectors enable rapid first-pass legal research and memo production beyond a model's training data.
pts.d: His IP example uses a proposed startup brand, Northwind, and a CourtListener connection to retrieve trademark-dispute opinions and related case information and produce a first-pass clearance memo. He contrasts an associate task that could take half a day with a demonstrated output taking approximately three or four minutes, possibly longer. He presents this as a draft capable of progressing to client use after partner review, not as independently validated or complete clearance.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The principal evidence is Barnes's short period of hands-on use and narrated demonstrations, supplemented by illustrative arithmetic and reported adoption examples.
pts.d: Barnes says he explored the release over the preceding 24–36 hours and shows installation, configuration, mock litigation intake and a trademark research workflow. His chronology time comparison is an estimate; no controlled comparison, accuracy benchmark or quantified review burden is supplied. Although he introduces Zapier as the easier demonstration path, he explicitly notes that the completed matter-creation workflow used the Clio MCP. As contextual evidence of legal interest and accessibility, he reports 20,000 registrations for an April webinar, Freshfields' co-innovation deal, Quinn Emanuel's internal platform and Thomson Reuters' use of the Claude agent SDK. These are Barnes's reported examples, not independently established findings in the transcript. He explicitly labels the suggestion that partnerships shaped the release as his inference.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: The claims concern immediately available capabilities at the release discussed in 2026, conditional on configuration, connectivity, permissions and attorney review.
pts.d: Barnes repeatedly places the launch 'yesterday'; the transcript gives no exact calendar date. He estimates installation at 15–20 seconds but separately says the initial practice interview takes 10–15 minutes. Customisation supplies jurisdiction, matter types, output formats and reviewer preferences. He acknowledges that 12 plugins do not cover every major practice area. Native connector availability varies: Clio and several other practice-management systems require a bridge. Zapier or community MCP use adds capability constraints, authentication, distribution effort and potentially additional cost. He recommends cybersecurity checks, sandbox testing and scrutiny of data residency, credentials, audit trails, code provenance, permissions and liability. His statement about ABA Opinion 512 and audit trails is expressly tentative and accompanied by his disclaimer that he is not a lawyer.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: Barnes identifies law firms, corporate legal departments, students and clinics as users, with production work shifting away from junior lawyers and technical responsibilities remaining with firms.
pts.d: For in-house counsel and GCs, he highlights contract review, NDAs, MSAs, M&A diligence, board minutes, entity compliance and employment workflows. For law firms, he emphasises litigation intake, chronology, drafting, privilege review and deposition preparation, alongside IP clearance and drafting. Junior associates' production time is the main target of his time-saving examples; partners retain judgment and review. Students receive study and bar-preparation tools, while clinics receive intake, deadline and supervisor-queue support. IT staff or engineers may need to vet and deploy non-native connections, with individual lawyers authenticating access. Clients are prospective recipients of reviewed outputs; Barnes does not quantify client fee reductions or access-to-justice effects.
